tables.title: COMPARISON OF MSE FOR THE PROPOSED AND TAYLOR-SERIES METHODS; LINEAR ARRAY AND DISTANT SOURCE
notes: B: Taylor series method. C: proposed method, (28) with Ψ = Q, (29). E: theoretical MSE of the new method = CRLB.

observations: The text states that for Tables III and IV, the source is far away at position (x⁰ = -50, y⁰ = 250), and sensor noise power is σ_j² = 0.00001/c² in both cases.
The text notes that when M is small (4 or 5), the proposed method has significantly less MSE than the Taylor-series method due to linearization errors.
The text mentions that the proposed method performs much better than SI and slightly better than Taylor-series for large M in Tables III and IV.
The text indicates that for the near-field case (Table II), the proposed method attains the CRLB for both linear and arbitrary array scenarios.
The text states that for distant source, the error is significant when the array base line is small (i.e., M is small), and as M increases, the base line increases, reducing linearization errors.

The text references DAC (Direct Approximation Criterion) being an optimum estimator around small error region, and that DAC gives an MSE in the order of 10⁶, even through the noise in the second case is smaller, because DAC requires a stochastic approximation which is only valid when transmitter position variance is small.
The text notes that although deviation from CRLB starts at high noise level, the MSE does not drop to a large value as compared to DAC.

The text states that the Bhattacharyya bound is tighter than CRLB for nonlinear parameter estimation, and that the method's performance is worse than the second-order Bhattacharyya bound (BHB2), possibly due to neglected second-order error terms.
uncertainties: Column 'MSE' in tables contains labels (e.g., 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E') rather than numerical MSE values; the actual MSE values are in the row entries under column headers like 'M = 3', etc. This is consistent across all tables, but may cause confusion if interpreted as numeric MSE in first column.
In Table II, row labels B, C, D, E correspond to different methods/conditions per note, but the table header says 'MSE' — the first column is actually method identifier, not MSE value.
